title: Pick one and own it: win positioning by owning a single advantage
summary: Jason Cohen proposes an exercise: imagine your company may have only one advantage over competitors, and build the whole sales talk-track around it. Focusing on one owned benefit sharpens the pitch, homepage, ads, demos and product, and he shows how a single advantage can answer a range of skeptical objections.

principles.text: Hang your hat on one advantage you can own completely; it beats diluting your message with many assertions.
principles.quote: Hanging your hat on just one advantage *that you can own completely* is stronger than diluting your message by making many assertions.

principles.text: Run the one-advantage exercise; it is a skill that pays off in every sales call, including defending against competitors or missing features.
principles.quote: You should go through this exercise because this skill is valuable in every sales call.

principles.text: A single focused advantage sharpens everything: homepage, ads, 30-second pitch, blog topics, demo, and your ideal customer.
principles.quote: Your homepage becomes laser-focused. Your advertisements become pointed, powerful, pithy, and other words starting with "p." Your 30-second pitch becomes compelling.

principles.text: Reframe objections through your one advantage. 'Most expensive' becomes the cost of failing, plus real support and expert help.
principles.quote: When you factor in the cost of the tool, also factor in the cost of *failing* to be successful with the tool.

principles.text: Counter the 'more features' objection: more bullet points often means worse features, and the real goal is solving the customer's specific needs.
principles.quote: Usually the more features a product has, the worse each feature is.

principles.text: Focus everything on one or two points: message, behavior, UX, product, target customer, and pitch. Don't try to defend ten.
principles.quote: Why try to defend ten points when you only need one or two to make your case?
